next_step: Leave rigid axis-seam origami entirely. The next live family must either use non-rigid within-piece maps, a non-fiber-preserving/base-mixing local model, or a construction whose discontinuity set does not map to boundary edges of the target simplex.
patterns_noticed: The key new pattern is local and exact. Every unit boundary edge of the triangular target simplex has only one incident unit triangle; this is true not only on `x1=0` and `x2=0` but also on the diagonal boundary. Interior edges have exactly two incident unit triangles. Combining that with attempt 012 yields a sharp separation: geometrically, any target boundary seam forces sheet coincidence because the boundary edge has only one adjacent triangle, while symplectically, only the coordinate axes are even eligible to hide derivative mismatch because only there does a torus factor collapse. So the coordinate axes are the only algebraically legal seams, yet they are still geometrically impossible for rigid origami. The path-level version is equally clean: a boundary axis path of length `L` meets `L` distinct unit triangles, so a rigid seam of length `L` on `x1=0` or `x2=0` forces at least `L` overlapping target triangles. When audited against attempt 013, every searched cut obeys this lower bound exactly or with slack; the slack ranges from 0 up to 16 in the saved artifact, with the tight cases occurring at the shallow one-edge cuts. This upgrades the search signal into a general rigid-family obstruction: any future piecewise-affine family that still relies on rigid target triangles and internal seams on boundary edges is structurally doomed, regardless of how many pieces it uses.
notes: No external literature was needed for this step because the obstruction is a direct combinatorial property of the triangular lattice and the target simplex. The script's conclusion is a mathematical inference from the verified local uniqueness mechanism and the exact incidence structure, not just another bounded search result.
